Generating ShortLex normal forms in affine A₂

A one-layer transformer generates ShortLex normal-form words in the affine Coxeter group Ã₂, one generator at a time. Each group element corresponds to a triangular region, called an alcove. Appending a generator reflects the current alcove across one of its walls, so the generated word can also be viewed as a walk through the triangular tiling.

The walk

The affine Coxeter group Ã₂ acts on a triangular tiling of the plane. Each group element corresponds to one triangle, called an alcove, and the identity is the shaded alcove marked e. Appending a generator g reflects the current alcove across its g-wall, so a word of length n becomes a chain of n triangles, each sharing an edge with the previous one.

Reduced words never revisit an alcove. If a sampled generator makes the word non-reduced, the walk visibly doubles back onto a triangle it has already visited.

The model

A 1-layer causal transformer with 4 attention heads, width 256, and no layer normalization was trained on 1,998 ShortLex normal-form words in Ã₂ of lengths 1 through 36. The data were split 30/70 into training and test sets. At each position, the model predicts one of four next tokens: stop, 1, 2, or 3.

Several generators may legally follow the same prefix, so exact next-token accuracy does not fully capture generation quality. A more informative test is whether the complete generated word remains in ShortLex normal form.

A word ends when the model emits stop or reaches the 36-letter cap. Across 513 distinct half-word seeds, the model stops on its own 356 times and reaches the cap 157 times. All 513 generated words are valid ShortLex normal forms, with lengths from 28 to 36.

Reading the panel

The bars show the model's probabilities for the next token. Legal means that appending the token keeps the word in ShortLex normal form. Legality is checked against all 1,998 normal-form words, rather than predicted by the model. When temperature is above 0, a tick on each bar marks the distribution used for sampling.

Length ℓ is the true Coxeter length of the prefix, or how far its alcove is from e. While the word remains reduced, this equals the number of letters in the prefix.
